title: Rank, Nullity, Sylvester and Frobenius
breadcrumb: Mathematics → Matrix algebra → Rank, nullity and the product inequalities
engineName: Mathematics — counting the independent directions a matrix carries
objectives: Give the equivalent definitions of rank and the bound rank ≤ min(m, n).
Apply rank–nullity with the column count, in both directions.
Read a rank off structure rather than by row reduction, including rows in arithmetic progression.

howto: Both of June 2026's questions on this topic are here, and neither needs much computation. Section 4 is Q26: difference the successive rows, see the arithmetic progression, and the rank is 2 in three subtractions — read that section before anything else, because the method transfers to every rank question the exam sets. Section 6 is Q1, derived rather than memorised: start from Sylvester's rank inequality and substitute υ = n − rank, remembering that subtraction reverses an inequality and turns min into max. Section 8 collects the product results and section 9 works the matrices a linear model needs, all by trace rather than by reduction. If short of time, sections 3, 4, 6 and 8 are the lesson. This lesson has no interactive chart: rank is a counting property rather than a curve, and no visualisation in the app illustrates it honestly. The optional section proves that row rank equals column rank and then makes Sylvester's inequality obvious as a counting argument, which is worth reading if the formula keeps slipping.

provenance: Authored November 2026, the first lesson of the maths module and the first to carry TWO PYQ anchors, because the catalog topic covers both. Q26 (wrong, marked C against B): the rank of a 4 × 4 matrix whose successive rows differ by the constant vector (1,1,0,0), so the rows are in arithmetic progression, the row space is span{R1, d}, and the rank is 2 with nullity 2 — confirmed three ways, from the rows, from the columns (C3 = 2C4 and C2 − C1 = C3) and by reduction, with determinant 0. Q1 (wrong, marked C against D): the nullity bounds on a product, max{υ(A), υ(B)} ≤ υ(AB) ≤ υ(A) + υ(B), which is Sylvester's rank inequality under υ = n − rank; the marked option's extra −n fails for A = B = I. The bounds were checked over 30,000 random 3 × 3 pairs with no violations and both ends frequently attained, and Sylvester's rank form over 20,000 random 4 × 4 pairs. Every other claim was computed: the ranks of the all-ones matrix, matrices with rows in arithmetic progression, the centring matrix at n = 4, 6, 10 (rank n−1, trace n−1, idempotent), rank(XᵀX) = rank(X), and the hat matrix and residual maker for a random 8 × 3 design (ranks 3 and 5, nullities 5 and 3). Skew-symmetric rank was checked over several thousand random matrices of orders 2 to 6: every non-zero rank observed was even. Two bank repairs were made while authoring: a Poisson interarrival item filed under Q26 in the maths variant file moved to the probability file under Q25, the seventh misfiling found in this bank; and four items under Q1 had contextless stems a learner could not answer, each given an explicit context chosen so the existing key is correct and verified BY CONSTRUCTION rather than by random search, which fails here because random integer matrices are almost always full rank. No explore scene: rank is a counting property and no visualisation in the app illustrates it honestly. Previous-year questions are stored separately and carry their exam cycle.

scenes.title: Before the lesson — four things it will assume
scenes.objective: Fix what rank and nullity are, and the one theorem that ties them together.

ask.q: A 4 × 4 matrix has rank 2. How many independent rows does it have, and how many independent columns?
ask.nudge: Rank has two apparently different definitions. Do they ever disagree?

body: Rank counts how much independent information a matrix carries. Everything else in this topic — nullity, singularity, estimability, multicollinearity — is a restatement of that count.

The single most useful fact is that the row count and the column count always agree: the maximum number of independent rows equals the maximum number of independent columns. So 'rank' is unambiguous, and you may compute it from whichever side is easier. For the exam's matrices, spotting a pattern in the rows is almost always easier than row-reducing.
Nullity is the complementary count — how much the matrix destroys. The rank–nullity theorem says the two add to the number of columns, so knowing one gives the other immediately.
Both of June 2026's questions on this topic were answered wrongly, and neither needed heavy computation: one needed a pattern spotted, the other needed one inequality rewritten. Four checks first.

items.ask: Define the rank of a matrix.
items.recall: The maximum number of linearly independent rows — equivalently, of columns. Equivalently the dimension of the row space, or of the column space.
refresh: Row rank equals column rank for every matrix, which is why one word suffices. The optional section explains why.
Equivalently: the number of non-zero rows in a row-reduced echelon form, or the order of the largest non-zero minor.
Practically, look for dependence before computing. Two proportional rows, a row of zeros, a column that is the sum of others — each drops the rank by one without any arithmetic.

items.ask: Do elementary row operations change the rank?
refresh: Swapping two rows, scaling a row by a non-zero constant, and adding a multiple of one row to another all leave the row space unchanged, so they leave its dimension unchanged.
That is precisely why row reduction is a legitimate way to FIND the rank — the whole method would be worthless otherwise.
One of the practice variants asks this directly. Note that scaling by ZERO is not an elementary operation, and it would destroy a row.

items.ask: For an m × n matrix, what is the largest the rank can be?
refresh: The rank cannot exceed the number of rows, nor the number of columns, so it is capped by the smaller. A 3 × 5 matrix has rank at most 3 — a practice variant.
A matrix attaining this cap is said to have full rank. A square matrix of full rank is non-singular, with non-zero determinant and an inverse.

So for a wide matrix the columns must be dependent: 5 columns in a 3-dimensional space cannot be independent. That observation is the whole of multicollinearity when there are more predictors than observations.

items.recall: For an m × n matrix A, rank(A) + nullity(A) = n, the number of COLUMNS.
refresh: Nullity is the dimension of the null space {x : Ax = 0}. Rank counts the directions A preserves; nullity counts the directions it crushes to zero.
So an n × n matrix of rank n − 1 has nullity 1, and a 10 × 10 matrix of rank 8 has nullity 2 — both practice variants, both one subtraction.
Mind that it is n, the column count, not m. For a 3 × 5 matrix of rank 3 the nullity is 5 − 3 = 2, not 0.

scenes.title: Rank is how many questions the data can answer
scenes.objective: See what a rank deficiency means before any algebra.
body: A matrix is usually standing in for a system: a design matrix of predictors, a set of equations, a transformation. Its rank says how many independent directions that system actually distinguishes.

If a design matrix has fewer independent columns than columns, some combination of the predictors is exactly reproducible from the others, and no amount of data will separate their effects. The computation does not fail politely — it fails by having infinitely many equally good answers, and software may return any one of them.

That is the practical meaning of nullity: the number of directions in which the parameters can be changed without changing the fit at all. Nullity zero means a unique answer; nullity 3 means a three-dimensional family of answers, all fitting identically.

Rank deficiency is also usually structural rather than accidental. A column of ones plus a full set of dummy variables for every category; a total column alongside its parts; two predictors recorded in different units. None of these are data problems; they are specification problems, and the rank is what reveals them.

scenario.teaser: A regression returns coefficients that change completely when the data are reordered.
scenario.title: The dummy variable trap, seen as a rank deficiency
body: An analyst models salary on an intercept plus four indicator columns, one for each of four departments. The software returns estimates, and a colleague running the same data on different software gets quite different coefficients. Both fits have identical residuals.

The design matrix has five columns, but the four department indicators sum to a column of ones — exactly the intercept column. So one column is a perfect linear combination of the others, the rank is 4, not 5, and the nullity of the design matrix is 1.

Nullity 1 means a one-dimensional family of coefficient vectors gives exactly the same fitted values: add any constant c to the intercept and subtract c from all four department effects, and nothing observable changes. The individual coefficients are not estimable; only certain contrasts between them are.

Different software picks a different member of that family — by dropping a column, by imposing a constraint, or by returning a generalised-inverse solution — which is why two correct programs disagree. Nothing is broken; the question as posed has no unique answer.

The repair is to remove the redundancy rather than to work around it: drop one indicator, or drop the intercept, or constrain the effects to sum to zero. Each gives a full-rank design and a unique answer, and each answers a slightly different question about what the remaining coefficients mean.

The general principle is worth stating plainly. X′X is invertible exactly when X has full column rank — and since rank(X′X) = rank(X), checking the rank of X settles it. A rank deficiency is not a numerical nuisance to be medicated with a tolerance setting; it is the model telling you that two of your questions are the same question.
scenario.q: Why do two correct programs return different coefficients, with identical residuals?
scenario.answer: Because the design matrix has nullity 1, so there is a whole line of coefficient vectors producing identical fitted values — the fit is unique, the coefficients are not. Adding c to the intercept and subtracting c from every department effect moves along that line and changes nothing observable. Each program resolves the indeterminacy differently (dropping a column, imposing a constraint, or taking a generalised inverse), so each reports a different point on the same line. The residuals agree because the fitted values are identical; the coefficients differ because they were never identified.

ask.q: A design matrix has 5 columns and rank 4. How many independent linear combinations of the coefficients ARE estimable?
ask.nudge: Estimable combinations correspond to directions the matrix preserves, not to the ones it crushes.

scenes.title: Rank, nullity, and how to find them without arithmetic
scenes.objective: State the definitions and the bounds, and learn to read rank off structure.

blocks.body:
For an m × n matrix A, rank(A) is
  • the maximum number of linearly independent rows,
  • the maximum number of linearly independent columns,
  • the dimension of the column space (the image of A), equivalently of the row space.
All three agree for every matrix. It also equals the number of non-zero rows in any row-reduced echelon form, and the order of the largest non-vanishing minor.

0 ≤ rank(A) ≤ min(m, n)
rank(A) = 0 only for the zero matrix.
A square n × n matrix is non-singular ⟺ rank = n ⟺ det ≠ 0 ⟺ nullity = 0 ⟺ A⁻¹ exists.
So a 3 × 5 matrix has rank at most 3, and a 5 × 5 matrix of rank 5 has non-zero determinant — two practice variants in one line.

rank(A) + υ(A) = n,  where n is the number of COLUMNS and υ denotes nullity.
υ(A) = dim{x : Ax = 0}. Consequences used constantly:
  rank n − 1 (square) ⟹ υ = 1;   10 × 10 of rank 8 ⟹ υ = 2;   υ(A) = 0 ⟹ A non-singular.

blocks.h: Read the rank off the structure, do not compute it
blocks.body:
Every exam matrix in this topic has visible dependence. Look for it in this order:
  1. A zero row or column.
  2. Two proportional rows or columns — rank of [[1,2],[2,4]] is 1, since R2 = 2R1.
  3. All rows equal, or all entries equal — the n × n matrix of ones has rank 1.
  4. One row or column equal to a combination of others.
  5. Rows in arithmetic progression — each row the previous plus a FIXED vector. Then every row lies in span{R1, d}, so the rank is at most 2 whatever the size.
Only if none of these appears should you row-reduce.

• n × n matrix of all ones: rank 1 (every row identical).
• Non-zero skew-symmetric (Aᵀ = −A): rank is always EVEN, so a non-zero skew-symmetric matrix cannot have rank 1 or 3.
• Idempotent (A² = A): rank(A) = trace(A). This is how ranks are found throughout linear models.
• Centring matrix C = I − (1/n)11ᵀ: idempotent with trace n − 1, so rank n − 1 and nullity 1 — it kills exactly the constant vector.
• rank(AᵀA) = rank(A) always, which is why X′X is invertible precisely when X has full column rank.

blocks.h: The nullity of a square matrix is the interesting half
blocks.body: For a square matrix the rank tells you whether the inverse exists; the nullity tells you how badly it does not. Nullity 1 means a one-dimensional family of solutions to Ax = 0, so Ax = b either has no solution or a one-parameter family of them. This is why the statistical content of this topic is almost entirely about nullity.

ask.q: If the rows of an n × n matrix are in arithmetic progression, the rank is at most 2 for every n. Why does the size not matter?
ask.nudge: Write row k as R1 + (k−1)d. How many vectors does every row lie in the span of?

scenes.title: Worked in full — June 2026, Q26
scenes.objective: Get the rank in one observation, then confirm it two other ways.

ask.q: The difference vector was (1,1,0,0), which has two zeros. Would the answer change if it had been (1,1,1,1)?
ask.nudge: What does the rank depend on — the entries of d, or the fact that there is a single fixed d?

steps.say: Before computing anything, difference successive rows.
steps.why: The same vector every time. So the rows are in arithmetic progression: Rₖ = R1 + (k−1)d with d = (1,1,0,0). This is the observation the whole question turns on, and it takes three subtractions.

steps.math:
every row lies in span{R1, d}
⟹ rank ≤ 2
R1 = (2,6,4,2) and d = (1,1,0,0) are not proportional
⟹ rank = 2
steps.why: Option B. The row space is spanned by two vectors, and they are independent, so the dimension is exactly 2. No row reduction was needed.

steps.say: Confirm from the columns, which must give the same answer.
steps.math:
C3 = (4,4,4,4),  C4 = (2,2,2,2)  ⟹ C3 = 2 C4
C2 − C1 = (4,4,4,4) = C3
⟹ at most 2 independent columns, and C1, C4 are independent
⟹ rank = 2 ✓
steps.why: Row rank equals column rank, so this is a genuine check rather than a repetition. Two separate dependencies among four columns leave two.

steps.say: Confirm by row reduction, for completeness.
steps.math:
R2−R1, R3−R1, R4−R1 give rows (1,1,0,0), (2,2,0,0), (3,3,0,0)
the last two are 2× and 3× the first
⟹ echelon form has 2 non-zero rows
⟹ rank = 2 ✓   and det = 0
steps.why: All three routes agree. The marked answer was 3, which is what comes of reducing carelessly and stopping with one spurious non-zero row — the risk the structural route avoids entirely.
One of the practice variants asks exactly this. Note it is the column count, which happens to equal the row count here only because the matrix is square.

scenes.after: The transferable move is differencing successive rows before anything else. It costs three subtractions and it either reveals an arithmetic progression — capping the rank at 2 however large the matrix — or it costs you nothing. Answering the question above: no, the entries of d are irrelevant; what matters is that a SINGLE fixed d works for every step.

scenes.title: Your turn — June 2026, Q1
scenes.objective: Derive the nullity bounds for a product from Sylvester's rank inequality.
scenes.problem: Let A and B be n × n matrices and let υ(·) denote nullity. Establish the correct bounds on υ(AB).

steps.say: Start from the rank side, where the standard results live.

blank.prompt: Give the two standard bounds on rank(AB).
blank.answer: rank(A) + rank(B) − n ≤ rank(AB) ≤ min{rank(A), rank(B)}
accept: Sylvester: rank(A)+rank(B)-n <= rank(AB) <= min of the two ranks
blank.hint: The upper bound says a product cannot be more informative than either factor; the lower bound is Sylvester's rank inequality.

steps.why: The upper bound holds because the image of AB sits inside the image of A, and its rank cannot exceed that of B either. The lower bound is Sylvester's inequality, sometimes called the Frobenius rank inequality in its three-factor form. Both were confirmed over 20,000 random 4 × 4 pairs with no violations.

steps.say: Convert the UPPER rank bound into a nullity statement.

blank.prompt: Apply υ = n − rank to rank(AB) ≤ min{rank(A), rank(B)}.
blank.hint: Subtracting from n reverses the inequality, and n − min{·} becomes max{n − ·}.

steps.why: n − rank(AB) ≥ n − min{rank A, rank B} = max{n − rank A, n − rank B} = max{υ(A), υ(B)}. A product can only ever destroy MORE than either factor alone, never less — which is the intuitive content of the lower bound on nullity.

steps.say: Now convert the LOWER rank bound.

blank.prompt: Apply υ = n − rank to rank(AB) ≥ rank(A) + rank(B) − n.
blank.hint: n − rank(AB) ≤ n − rank(A) − rank(B) + n. Group the terms as two nullities.

steps.why: n − rank(AB) ≤ 2n − rank(A) − rank(B) = (n − rank A) + (n − rank B) = υ(A) + υ(B). The nullities are sub-additive: the product cannot destroy more than the two factors destroy between them.

steps.say: Put the two together and pick the option.

blank.hint: Combine the two inequalities you just derived.

steps.why: Option D, the official answer. The marked option C put υ(A) + υ(B) − n as the upper bound, which is strictly smaller and fails immediately: take A = B = I, so υ(A) = υ(B) = 0 and υ(AB) = 0, while the claimed bound is −n, and 0 ≤ −n is false.

steps.say: Check that the interval is not merely valid but tight.

blank.prompt: For 6 × 6 matrices with υ(A) = 3 and υ(B) = 2, what interval does the result give?
blank.hint: max{3, 2} at the bottom and 3 + 2 at the top.

steps.why: Exactly [3, 5], and neither end can be improved: A = diag(1,1,1,0,0,0) with B = diag(1,1,1,1,0,0) gives υ(AB) = 3, while choosing B whose image contains the whole null space of A gives υ(AB) = 5. Both were constructed and verified, which is how you know the answer is the sharpest true statement rather than just a true one.

scenes.after: The method generalises: when a result about nullities is wanted and you only remember the rank version, substitute υ = n − rank and remember that subtracting reverses the inequality and turns min into max. That single move converts Sylvester into the answer here, and it is quicker than memorising both forms.

scenes.title: Sylvester, Frobenius, and the ranks that statistics needs
scenes.objective: Collect the product results and the matrices built from a design matrix.

blocks.body:
For three factors,
    rank(AB) + rank(BC) ≤ rank(B) + rank(ABC).
Sylvester is the special case with B = I. It is the result the syllabus names alongside Sylvester, and it is rarely needed numerically — recognising the name is usually enough.

Both ends are reachable, which is why the statement cannot be sharpened. With 5 × 5 matrices of rank 3 each, Sylvester's floor is 3 + 3 − 5 = 1, and rank(AB) = 1 is achieved by arranging the image of B to contain the whole null space of A. The upper bound min{3,3} = 3 is achieved whenever the image of B misses the null space of A entirely — the generic case, which is why random examples almost always sit at the top.

blocks.h: Ranks built from a design matrix
blocks.body:
Let X be n × k with full column rank k.
    rank(XᵀX) = rank(X) = k, so XᵀX is invertible exactly when X has full column rank.
    hat matrix H = X(XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀ:   idempotent, trace k, so rank k and nullity n − k.
    residual maker M = I − H:      idempotent, trace n − k, so rank n − k and nullity k.
The nullity of the residual maker is k — one of the practice variants, and it is k because M annihilates exactly the column space of X.

If A² = A then every eigenvalue is 0 or 1, the rank counts the eigenvalues equal to 1, and the trace sums them — so rank(A) = trace(A). This turns every rank question about H, M and the centring matrix into a trace computation, which is far easier. The centring matrix I − (1/n)11ᵀ has trace n − 1·(1/n)·n... more directly, trace = n − 1, hence rank n − 1 and nullity 1.

If Aᵀ = −A then the non-zero eigenvalues come in conjugate imaginary pairs ±iλ, so there is an even number of them and the rank is even. A non-zero skew-symmetric matrix therefore cannot have rank 1, and a 3 × 3 one has rank exactly 2. Checked over several thousand random skew-symmetric matrices of orders 2 to 6: every observed rank was 2, 4 or 6, never odd.

ask.q: rank(XᵀX) = rank(X) for every real X. Why does that make the invertibility of XᵀX a question purely about X?
ask.nudge: XᵀX is k × k. When is a k × k matrix invertible, in terms of its rank?

scenes.title: On your own — the statistical matrices, by trace
scenes.objective: Compute the ranks a linear model needs, using idempotence rather than reduction.
scenes.problem: Take n = 8 observations and a design matrix X of order 8 × 3 with full column rank 3. Find the rank and nullity of (a) XᵀX, (b) the hat matrix H = X(XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀ, (c) the residual maker M = I − H, and (d) the centring matrix C = I − (1/8)11ᵀ.
hints: For (a), use rank(AᵀA) = rank(A). Note XᵀX is 3 × 3, so rank–nullity uses 3.
For (b), (c) and (d), check idempotence first — then the rank is just the trace.
Collapse trace(X(XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀ) with trace(AB) = trace(BA) to get a 3 × 3 trace.
scenes.answer: (a) rank 3, nullity 0. (b) rank 3, nullity 5. (c) rank 5, nullity 3. (d) rank 7, nullity 1.
scenes.check: Three things to be exact about. In (a) the nullity is 0 because XᵀX is 3 × 3 of rank 3, not 8 − 3. In (c) the NULLITY of the residual maker is 3 = k, while its rank is 5 = n − k; stating those the wrong way round is the standard slip and it is exactly what one of the practice variants tests. And every rank here came from a trace only because all four matrices are idempotent — rank = trace is not a general fact, and it fails for the Q26 matrix, which has trace 15 and rank 2.

scenario.teaser: An analyst adds two predictors, and the residual degrees of freedom do not drop by two.
scenario.title: Degrees of freedom are ranks, not column counts
body: A model with 40 observations and 5 predictors plus an intercept reports 34 residual degrees of freedom. The analyst adds two more predictors and expects 32, but the software reports 33.

The reason is that one of the two new columns was a linear combination of columns already present — a ratio reconstructable from two existing variables, say. The design matrix gained two columns but only one rank, so the residual degrees of freedom fell by one rather than two.

This is not a quirk of the software. The residual degrees of freedom are literally the rank of the residual maker I − H, which is n − rank(X). It is the rank of the design matrix that counts, never the number of columns, and the two differ precisely when the columns are dependent.

The same identity explains the arithmetic of every analysis of variance table. Model degrees of freedom are rank(H), residual degrees of freedom are rank(I − H), and they add to n because the two idempotent matrices split the space into orthogonal complements. Nothing in that depends on how many columns were written down.

The practical reading of the discrepancy is a warning, not a nuisance: the model contains a redundancy the analyst did not intend. The coefficient on at least one of the new predictors is not estimable, and the software has silently resolved the ambiguity — by dropping a column or by using a generalised inverse — rather than refusing to fit.

So a degrees-of-freedom count that does not match expectation is the cheapest available check on a design matrix. If the number is one too high, a column is redundant, and the fix is to find out which and why.
scenario.q: Why did adding two columns cost only one degree of freedom?
scenario.answer: Because residual degrees of freedom are n − rank(X), and the rank counts independent columns rather than columns. One of the two new columns lay in the span of the existing ones, so the rank rose by one while the column count rose by two. The degrees of freedom are the rank of the idempotent matrix I − H, which is n − rank(X) exactly — so a count that is one higher than expected is a direct report that the design matrix has a dependency in it.

solution.math:
XᵀX is 3 × 3
rank(XᵀX) = rank(X) = 3  ⟹ full rank ⟹ invertible
υ(XᵀX) = 3 − 3 = 0
solution.why: Full rank, so the normal equations have a unique solution and the inverse in H exists. Had X had rank 2, XᵀX would be singular and the model not estimable — the scenario from section 2.

solution.math:
H² = X(XᵀX)⁻¹XᵀX(XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀ = X(XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀ = H, so H is idempotent
trace(H) = trace(X(XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀ) = trace((XᵀX)⁻¹XᵀX) = trace(I₃) = 3
⟹ rank(H) = 3,  υ(H) = 8 − 3 = 5
solution.why: The trace step uses trace(AB) = trace(BA) to collapse an 8 × 8 trace into a 3 × 3 one. Verified numerically: rank 3 and trace 3.0000 for a random 8 × 3 X of rank 3.

solution.math:
M = I − H is idempotent too: M² = I − 2H + H² = I − H = M
trace(M) = 8 − 3 = 5
⟹ rank(M) = 5,  υ(M) = 8 − 5 = 3 = k
solution.why: The nullity of M is exactly k = 3, because M annihilates precisely the column space of X, which is 3-dimensional. That is the practice variant's answer, and note it is k rather than n − k — easy to state backwards.

solution.math:
C = I − (1/8)11ᵀ is idempotent
trace(C) = 8 − (1/8)·trace(11ᵀ) = 8 − (1/8)(8) = 7
⟹ rank(C) = 7,  υ(C) = 8 − 7 = 1
solution.why: In general rank n − 1 and nullity 1: C kills exactly the constant vectors, which form a one-dimensional space, and preserves everything orthogonal to them. Verified at n = 4, 6 and 10 — rank n − 1, trace n − 1, idempotent in each case.

solution.math:
degrees of freedom: model 3 = rank(H), residual 5 = rank(M), total 8
3 + 5 = 8
solution.why: The ranks of H and M are the model and residual degrees of freedom, and they add to n because H and M decompose the space into orthogonal complements. Every degrees-of-freedom count in analysis of variance is a rank computed this way.

scenes.title: Six statements — verdict on each before you look
scenes.objective: Rule on the claims the variants on this topic are built from.
scenes.intro: Decide true or false on all six before revealing any.

items.claim: Elementary row operations can change the rank of a matrix.
items.why: False — they preserve it exactly, which is the only reason row reduction can be used to find a rank. Row swaps, non-zero scalings and adding a multiple of one row to another all leave the row space unchanged.

items.claim: rank(A) + nullity(A) equals the number of rows of A.
items.why: False — it equals the number of COLUMNS. For a 3 × 5 matrix of rank 3 the nullity is 5 − 3 = 2, not 0. The confusion is harmless for square matrices and wrong for every other shape.

items.claim: A non-zero skew-symmetric matrix can have rank 1.
items.why: False. The non-zero eigenvalues of a skew-symmetric matrix come in conjugate imaginary pairs, so the rank is always even. A non-zero 3 × 3 skew-symmetric matrix has rank exactly 2.

items.claim: If A is idempotent then rank(A) = trace(A).
items.why: True. Idempotence forces every eigenvalue to be 0 or 1; the rank counts the ones and the trace sums them. This is how the ranks of the hat matrix, the residual maker and the centring matrix are found.

items.claim: For every real matrix A, rank(AᵀA) = rank(A).
items.why: True, and it is why XᵀX is invertible exactly when X has full column rank. It holds for real matrices because Ax = 0 and AᵀAx = 0 have the same solutions: AᵀAx = 0 implies xᵀAᵀAx = ‖Ax‖² = 0.

items.claim: υ(AB) ≤ υ(A) + υ(B) − n for n × n matrices A and B.
items.why: False, and it is the option marked in June 2026. The correct upper bound is υ(A) + υ(B) with no subtraction. Take A = B = I: then υ(A) = υ(B) = υ(AB) = 0, and the claim reads 0 ≤ −n, which is absurd.

scenes.title: On your own — six quick ranks
scenes.objective: Apply the structural shortcuts at speed.
scenes.problem: Give the rank, and where asked the nullity. (a) [[1,2],[2,4]]. (b) The 6 × 6 matrix of all ones, with its nullity. (c) A 3 × 5 matrix — the largest its rank can be, and the nullity if it attains that. (d) A 10 × 10 matrix of rank 8 — its nullity. (e) A square matrix with υ(A) = 0 — what can be said about it. (f) Two 5 × 5 matrices of rank 3 each — the smallest rank(AB) can be.
hints: For (a) and (b), look for proportional or identical rows.
For (c), the cap is min(m, n), and rank–nullity uses the COLUMN count.
For (f), use Sylvester's lower bound, then ask whether it is actually attainable.
scenes.answer: (a) 1. (b) rank 1, nullity 5. (c) rank at most 3, nullity 2. (d) nullity 2. (e) non-singular — invertible, det ≠ 0, full rank. (f) 1.
scenes.check: Two traps here. In (c) the nullity is 5 − 3 = 2 because there are five columns; answering 0 means using the row count. In (f) Sylvester gives rank(AB) ≥ 3 + 3 − 5 = 1, but a bound is only an answer if it is attained — and it is: put the image of B so that it contains the whole 2-dimensional null space of A, and A destroys two of B's three image dimensions, leaving 1. Random examples will not find it, since generically rank(AB) = 3.

solution.why: A 2 × 2 matrix of rank 1 has determinant zero: 1·4 − 2·2 = 0, which is the same observation.
The row space is one-dimensional, so the null space is five-dimensional — it is every vector whose entries sum to zero.

solution.math:
rank ≤ min(3, 5) = 3
if rank = 3 then υ = 5 − 3 = 2
solution.why: Five columns in a space of dimension 3 cannot be independent, so there are always at least two independent solutions to Ax = 0.
One subtraction. The matrix crushes a two-dimensional subspace to zero.

solution.math:
υ(A) = 0 ⟹ rank = n ⟹ non-singular
⟹ det ≠ 0, A⁻¹ exists, Ax = 0 only for x = 0
solution.why: All four statements are the same statement. 'Non-singular' is the word the options use.
Verified by explicit construction. The null space of A is span{e₄, e₅}, and the image of B contains both, so A annihilates two of the three dimensions B produces.

scenes.title: Where rank decides the statistics
scenes.objective: Recognise rank conditions across the rest of the syllabus.

blocks.body: βˆ = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy exists exactly when X has full column rank, because rank(XᵀX) = rank(X). When it does not, only certain linear combinations cᵀβ are estimable — those with c in the row space of X — and the rest are not identified at all, however much data there is.

Model and residual degrees of freedom ARE ranks: rank(H) = k and rank(I − H) = n − k, and they sum to n because the two matrices decompose the space. Every ANOVA table is a rank decomposition, and the chi-square degrees of freedom in the associated distribution theory are these same ranks.

When XᵀX is singular a generalised inverse supplies A solution rather than THE solution, and the dimension of the solution family is the nullity. That is the formal version of the dummy-variable scenario: nullity 1 means a one-parameter family, and different software picks different members.

The rank of a covariance matrix is the number of dimensions the distribution really occupies: a singular covariance matrix means the data lie in a lower-dimensional subspace exactly. Principal component analysis counts non-zero eigenvalues, which is the rank, and a quadratic form's rank is the number of non-zero coefficients in its diagonalised version.

Every one of these asks the same question: how many independent directions does this matrix distinguish? Rank answers it, nullity answers the complement, and rank–nullity converts between them. The statistical consequences — unique estimates, correct degrees of freedom, identifiability — all follow from that one count.

ask.q: A covariance matrix of 5 variables has rank 3. What does that say about the data, exactly?
ask.nudge: Nullity 2 means two independent directions get crushed. What does a direction of zero variance mean?

scenes.title: Second recall — the parts most likely to fade
scenes.objective: Retrieve the product bounds and the named matrices.

items.q: State Sylvester's rank inequality, being careful which dimension is subtracted.
items.a: rank(A) + rank(B) − n ≤ rank(AB) ≤ min{rank(A), rank(B)}, where n is the SHARED dimension.

items.q: Give the bounds on υ(AB) for n × n matrices.
items.a: max{υ(A), υ(B)} ≤ υ(AB) ≤ υ(A) + υ(B) — June 2026 Q1, option D.

items.q: Why is the upper bound NOT υ(A) + υ(B) − n?
items.a: Because A = B = I gives 0 ≤ −n, which is false.

items.q: Rank and nullity of the centring matrix I − (1/n)11ᵀ?
items.a: Rank n − 1, nullity 1 — it kills exactly the constant vectors.

items.q: Nullity of the residual maker I − X(XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀ, for X of order n × k and rank k?
items.a: k, because it annihilates precisely the k-dimensional column space of X.

items.q: What is the rank of a non-zero skew-symmetric matrix?

scenes.title: What you should now be able to do unaided
scenes.objective: Close the loop before the mastery test.
body: Give the three equivalent definitions of rank and the bound rank ≤ min(m, n).
Use rank–nullity with the COLUMN count, in both directions.
Read a rank off structure: proportional rows, all-ones, rows in arithmetic progression.
Answer June 2026 Q26 in three subtractions, and confirm it from the columns.
State Sylvester's rank inequality and convert it into the nullity bounds of June 2026 Q1.
Dismiss the υ(A) + υ(B) − n bound with the A = B = I counterexample.
Use rank = trace for idempotent matrices to get the ranks of H, I − H and the centring matrix.
Say why rank(XᵀX) = rank(X) settles estimability in a linear model.

scenes.title: Why row rank equals column rank
scenes.objective: See the one proof that makes the whole topic coherent.

blocks.body: A 3 × 100 matrix has 3 rows and 100 columns. That the maximum number of independent rows equals the maximum number of independent columns is a genuine theorem, not a definition, and it is the reason 'rank' can be a single number rather than two.

blocks.h: The factorisation proof, in four lines
blocks.body:
Let r be the row rank, and let v₁, …, v_r be a basis of the row space. Every row of A is a combination of them, so
    A = C R,
where R is r × n with the vᵢ as its rows and C is m × r holding the coefficients.
Now read A = CR by columns: every column of A is a combination of the r columns of C. So the column space has dimension at most r, giving column rank ≤ row rank.
Apply the same argument to Aᵀ to get row rank ≤ column rank. The two are equal.

blocks.h: Rank as the dimension of the image
blocks.body: The cleanest statement is geometric: A maps ℝⁿ to ℝᵐ, and rank(A) is the dimension of the image. Rank–nullity is then the statement that the domain splits into what gets crushed (dimension υ) and what survives (dimension rank), and υ + rank = n because those two account for every direction in ℝⁿ.

blocks.h: Why the product bounds are now obvious
blocks.body:
AB first applies B, landing in the image of B, then applies A. The result's dimension cannot exceed the dimension of the image of B, giving rank(AB) ≤ rank(B); and it lies inside the image of A, giving rank(AB) ≤ rank(A). For the lower bound, A can destroy at most υ(A) = n − rank(A) dimensions of B's image, so
    rank(AB) ≥ rank(B) − υ(A) = rank(A) + rank(B) − n,
which IS Sylvester's inequality, now visibly a counting argument rather than a formula.

blocks.h: And why the bounds are tight
blocks.body: The lower bound is attained exactly when the image of B contains as much of the null space of A as it can. That is what the explicit 5 × 5 construction in section 9 arranges, and it is why random examples never find it: two subspaces in general position intersect as little as possible, which puts rank(AB) at the TOP of its range. Extremes in this topic always have to be built, never sampled.

ask.q: Reading rank as the dimension of the image, why can rank(AB) never exceed rank(B)?
ask.nudge: AB applies B first. What space is the input to A restricted to?

scenes.objective: Demonstrate it independently, on questions you have not seen.
